title: Ines and the Cellar
premise: Hazel Amberdale takes a private hospice case at Marrow House, caring for the dying matriarch Edith Vane, who insists she will not sign her inheritance papers until 'the guest' leaves. Hazel, a rationalist who has heard too many dying patients count backwards to be comforted by coincidence, dismisses the house's wrongness until its mirrors begin lagging one second behind reality — and something in that stolen second begins noticing her. As night falls and Edith's estranged heirs arrive to force the signature, Hazel uncovers the truth: decades ago the Vane family invited something into the cellar as collateral for their fortune, and the inheritance papers are not a will but a renewal of the invitation. To survive until sunrise, Hazel must choose between loyalty to her patient and exposing the truth that will destroy the Vane name — burning the papers in the cellar itself, freeing Edith to die at dawn while the house, uninvited, forgets them all.
about_author: Wendell Underhill is the pen name of a former estate lawyer from coastal Maine who spent twenty years probating houses no one wanted to enter. He writes horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the terrible things families keep in basements.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Introducing her habit of hearing dying patients count backwards, she arrives at fog-bound Marrow House to care for Edith Vane, who refuses food, medicine, and most urgently the lawyers' papers. The emotional beat is wary professionalism masking unease; the chapter ends with Edith whispering that the house must never hear Hazel say her own name aloud.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Settling into the nurse's quarters, she notices her reflection blinks after she does — then all mirrors in the house lag exactly one second behind. Rational explanations fail one by one. The beat is creeping denial; she tapes a bedsheet over the hallway mirror and tells herself it's dust, fatigue, anything but belief.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, lucid for the first time. She recounts 1974: her husband's failing business, the stranger in the cellar, the contract signed in a ledger still kept below. Every thirty years the invitation renews; this time the renewal is hidden inside the inheritance papers. The beat is confession as plea — Edith begs Hazel to keep the heirs from signing anything tonight.

chapters.title: The Heirs Arrive
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Edith's three adult children arrive before dusk, impatient, grieving in ugly ways, each carrying their own copy of the papers and a hunger for the house. The lawyer among them, Marcus, notices Hazel's questions and grows cold. The beat is social dread — the true horror is familial greed sharpening against a dying woman's last wish.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Alternating Hazel and youngest heir Sylvie's POVs. Sylvie, the only heir who loved Edith, finds the cellar door unlocked though it was nailed shut in her childhood. Below: the ledger, candle stubs arranged in a ring, and a smell like a room remembering being occupied. The beat is forbidden curiosity rewarded with terror; they flee as something climbs the stairs behind them at a patient pace.

chapters.title: Sunset Clause
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The lawyer reveals he has read the fine print of his own firm's founding documents and knows what the papers renew — and intends to sign anyway, trading the family's soul-debt for sole inheritance. He locks Hazel in the linen room. The beat is betrayal; loyalty curdles as Hazel realizes the danger was never only below the floorboards.

chapters.title: The Second That Watches
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, escaping through the service passage. The mirror-lag worsens: now reflections act independently, showing versions of the family that stayed loyal, that told the truth, that burned the ledger years ago. The entity uses these second-late selves as bait. The beat is psychological siege — Hazel must decide which reflection, if any, is hers.

chapters.title: Signature
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging in Edith's bedroom at midnight. Marcus presents the papers; Edith, dying, cannot lift the pen; the eldest heir signs on her behalf — and every mirror in the house shatters except one, which begins filling with dark water. The beat is catastrophe; the invitation renews, and the thing in the cellar starts climbing toward the light it was promised.

chapters.title: Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, climax. With Sylvie's help she carries the ledger and papers down into the cellar, past the rising guest, and burns them in the old candle ring while reciting the revocation clause Edith taught her. The entity demands a name in trade; Hazel gives it Edith's instead of her own — loyalty and truth fused into one act. The beat is sacrificial defiance against the clock.

chapters.title: Dawn, Uninherited
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, resolution. Edith dies peacefully at first light, unsigned and free, counting forwards for once. The mirrors reflect in real time; the house stands empty and ordinary, its fortune legally voided, the heirs left with nothing but each other. Hazel walks out past the open cellar door, which shows only stairs. Final beat: quiet grief, hard-won justice outside any law, and a hospice nurse who still doesn't believe — but no longer needs to.
